scope: Focused literature follow-up and identity corrections. Absence from this file means no dedicated paper review yet, not absence of published evidence.

wds20591+0418c.png.name: ε Equulei AB
wds20591+0418c.png.finding: ORB6 prints HIP 103579, an unrelated HD 200019 star at declination +44.79 degrees. HIP 103569 has HD 199766 and coordinates matching the ORB6 source position at +04.29 degrees. Preserve the printed identifier as provenance and use HIP 103569 for future component work.
wds20591+0418c.png.nextStep: Review the AB subsystem, mass ratio and barycentric motion using the corrected identity.

wds04301+1538c.png.name: 80 Tauri
wds04301+1538c.png.finding: Torres (2019) derives component masses of 1.63 and 1.11 solar masses and a barycentric proper motion of +106.41, -25.72 mas/yr. Resolved Gaia positions can supply an absolute anchor at their actual reference epoch. The grade-3 relative orbit remains an adopted model with appreciable parameter uncertainty.
wds04301+1538c.png.nextStep: Build and validate a resolved-component barycentre with the published systemic motion; keep systemic RV unknown unless independently established.

wds21145+1000a.png.name: δ Equulei
wds21145+1000a.png.finding: PHASES combined visual and double-lined RV solutions determine component masses and distance precisely. Hipparcos AstroRef=* is a photocentre solution, so it must not be used directly as a barycentre or combined with the relative orbit without accounting for photocentre motion.
wds21145+1000a.png.nextStep: Obtain a reviewed absolute barycentric solution or reconstruct the photocentre position and mission-averaged proper motion using the correct bandpass flux ratio.

wds15232+3017a.png.name: η Coronae Borealis AB
wds15232+3017a.png.finding: The PHASES combined solution gives masses 1.243 and 1.100 solar masses and distance 18.50 pc. A distant brown-dwarf companion is outside the AB orbit. An AB-only model needs an explicit scope and an absolute barycentre anchor.
wds15232+3017a.png.nextStep: Review absolute component astrometry and confirm which identifiers belong to A and B before adopting the PHASES mass ratio.

wds09006+4147a.png.name: 10 Ursae Majoris (HD 76943)
wds09006+4147a.png.finding: Söderhjelm Table 1 provides an astrometric mass ratio, unlike the photometric estimates in Tables 3–4. The Hipparcos main solution is not explicitly barycentric. PHASES discusses the limited available RV measurements.
wds09006+4147a.png.nextStep: Reconcile the published astrometric mass ratio with the adopted orbit and recover barycentric position and proper motion.

wds17349+1234c.png.name: α Ophiuchi (Rasalhague)
wds17349+1234c.png.finding: Gardner et al. (2021) combine imaging, interferometry and RVs to derive a precision orbit and component masses. This supplies much stronger mass evidence than a brightness-based estimate; it does not by itself identify a usable absolute barycentre solution.
wds17349+1234c.png.nextStep: Retain the paper's adopted distance, mass ratio, node convention and systemic motion together; obtain a compatible absolute position anchor.

wds18070+3034a.png.name: 99 Herculis
wds18070+3034a.png.finding: Kennedy et al. (2012) adopt component masses 0.94 and 0.46 solar masses, using the spectroscopic mass function; they also discuss a previously suspected third component and an unbound wide C star. Hipparcos AstroRef=A is a component position, with orbital motion present in its proper motion.
wds18070+3034a.png.nextStep: Recover a consistent systemic proper motion and barycentric position. Correcting only the component-A position would leave orbital motion counted in the proper motion.

wds00022+2705b.png.name: 85 Pegasi
wds00022+2705b.png.finding: The secondary has been discussed as a close binary in published stellar-model calibrations. The S99 photometric ratio alone is not a secure subsystem mass ratio. Hipparcos has a stochastic X solution rather than an explicit barycentre.
wds00022+2705b.png.nextStep: Reconcile the A–(Ba+Bb) mass budget and absolute astrometry; distinguish measured dynamical constraints from stellar-model masses and proposed companions.

wds21446+2539a.png.name: κ Pegasi
wds21446+2539a.png.finding: PHASES explicitly models a triple system, including the short-period Ba–Bb pair. The visual A–B orbit requires the total B-subsystem mass, not the mass of its brighter member. Hipparcos is a photocentre solution.
wds21446+2539a.png.nextStep: Use subsystem masses and define whether the model tracks a subsystem barycentre or its photocentre; validate the absolute anchor and motion.

wds00352-0336c.png.name: 13 Ceti
wds00352-0336c.png.finding: The visual primary is a short-period spectroscopic binary. S99 flags the system and supplies an astrometric mass ratio for the visual pair; this cannot be interpreted as two single-star masses without specifying the hierarchy.
wds00352-0336c.png.nextStep: Review the modern combined orbit and subsystem masses, then reconstruct the correct absolute reference point.

wds14514+1906i.png.name: ξ Bootis
wds14514+1906i.png.finding: Both the angular orbit and the nearby distance are promising, but S99 Table 3's quoted ratio is photometric. Hipparcos AstroRef=A includes the primary's orbital motion. Resolved component astrometry offers a route to a mass-weighted absolute solution.
wds14514+1906i.png.nextStep: Review a measured mass ratio and the two resolved Gaia solutions, including their source identities, actual epochs and astrometric quality.

wds02039+4220a.png.name: γ Andromedae BC (Almach subsystem)
wds02039+4220a.png.finding: The ORB6 designation explicitly describes BC, while HIP 9640 and the existing Almach chart row identify the bright A component. A positional cross-match at the system level cannot assign A's aliases or astrometry to B.
wds02039+4220a.png.nextStep: Identify B and C separately and reconstruct their subsystem barycentre; retain the bright A chart star independently.
